_notes: Provenance oracle for Stage A (BLUEPRINT 5.1). Every jd_quote, alt_quote and other_grounded_sentence is a verbatim sentence of the named JD file (UTF-8, LF, no BOM). jd_quote_offset is [start, end) into that file's text: jd[start:end] == jd_quote, and the sentence occurs exactly once. Offsets are computed in code after the substring match (brain/rubric.py maps the normalised match back to raw offsets); never ask the model for them.

gate_norm is the normalisation the gate must apply to BOTH the quote and the JD: unicodedata.normalize('NFKC', s), then translate every key of gate_norm.translate to its value, then collapse whitespace runs to one space, strip, lower-case. This deliberately extends the BLUEPRINT 5.1 sketch (whitespace + lower only): real pasted JDs carry U+2019 apostrophes, U+2013 en dashes, U+2011 hyphens and U+00A0 spaces while the model emits ASCII, and jd_fintech_unicode.txt proves the plain sketch silently drops such quotes (unicode_variants.must_fail_under_plain_norm). Record the deviation in docs/DECISIONS.md.

Degenerate quotes: the sketch's `norm(q) in jd_n` accepts '' (always True), 'you', '- ' and 'Node.js' as grounded. The gate must additionally require len(gate_norm(q).split()) >= min_quote_words. min_quote_words is 3, not higher, because the BLUEPRINT 5.2 example why-trace quotes 'optimise API latency' (3 words) and that must stay legal. degenerate_quotes_must_be_rejected are quotes that ARE plain substrings of the JD and must still be rejected.

Matching a rubric competency to an oracle entry: competency names are free text, so match on quotes. Take the competency's jd_quotes in order. A quote q matches an entry when, after gate_norm and stripping a leading bullet marker ('- ', '* ', '1.') and trailing punctuation, len(q.split()) >= min_match_words and q is a substring of the entry's jd_quote or of one of its alt_quotes (or contains one of them). The first quote that matches any entry decides; a competency matches at most one entry and an entry may be matched by more than one competency. fragment_examples_that_match are grounded fragments a 9B model actually returns (leading 'You will' dropped, bullet prefix kept, trailing period dropped) and must match their entry. Keyword shortcut: every quote of an entry contains one of its match_keywords and no keyword of one entry occurs in another entry's quotes (verify_fixtures.py enforces both), so `any(k in gate_norm(q) for k in match_keywords)` is an equivalent lookup.

Assert that at least min_entries_matched entries are matched by the rubric, not all of them: a correct 5-8 competency rubric can legitimately merge or omit entries. type and priority on entries are advisory; on the rubric as a whole assert only expected_mix (at least behavioral_count_min competencies typed behavioral, i.e. behavioral fraction >= behavioral_min).

domain_terms: at least min_domain_terms_hit of them must appear in the rubric JSON or in the first three questions; every domain_term is absent from the other JD (that half is what verify_fixtures.py enforces, and it is what makes the swap-the-JD difference visible).

paraphrase_that_must_be_rejected are near-paraphrases of real JD sentences; validate_rubric must drop a competency whose only quotes are these, and with three such competencies needs_reask() must be True.
shared_title and shared_seniority are identical across both JDs by design: the only thing that should make the two rubrics differ is the JD body.
